property_summary: For any sender S and value v, after S calls addToBalance() paying v, the contract's userBalance for key S increases by v; the mutant updates userBalance[tx.origin] instead, so when msg.sender != tx.origin the mutant can leave userBalance[msg.sender] unchanged and thus violate this rule.

For any caller A and any ETH amount v they send via addToBalance(), the reference contract increases userBalance[A] by v (so getBalance(A) after the call equals previous + v); the mutant increments userBalance[tx.origin] instead, so when msg.sender != tx.origin (i.e. a call proxied through another contract) the mutant can leave userBalance[msg.sender] unchanged and break the rule.

For any caller and any ETH amount, calling addToBalance on the correct contract always increases that caller's stored userBalance by exactly the sent msg.value (i.e., userBalance[msg.sender] after == before + msg.value); the mutant removes the check and can cause balances to diverge (e.g., due to overflow) so this equality can be violated for some inputs.

For any caller and any sent amount, after addToBalance completes the contract's public getter getBalance for any address k will never report a balance less than its previous value (balances are monotonic non-decreasing); the mutant can violate this monotonicity for some fuzzed inputs by allowing overflow/incorrect checks so a balance can decrease for some key.

For any caller A and any amount v (0 <= v <= type(uint256).max), a successful call to addToBalance by A always increases A's stored balance by exactly v in the reference; the mutant can make the stored balance of A differ (due to unchecked overflow) for some fuzzed A and v.

For every caller and any sent amount, calling addToBalance on the correct contract never decreases the balance of any address compared to before the call (i.e., for all k: getBalance(k) after >= getBalance(k) before); the mutant's removed check can allow an overflow that makes some address's reported balance smaller for some inputs.

Invariant: for any sender S and any sent amount v, after addToBalance() on the correct contract, the stored balance of every address k equals the previous stored balance of k plus any successful outgoing transfer that actually cleared from the contract (i.e., balances of OTHER addresses never increase as a side-effect of S calling addToBalance); the mutant can corrupt unrelated keys so some other address's balance can change after a call to addToBalance by S (the bug allows overflow/incorrect accounting and can arbitrarily change stored slots).

For every caller and value, calling addToBalance with value v never decreases any account's stored userBalance (i.e., userBalance[k] after the call is >= before) in the reference; deleting the require can overflow and cause some key's balance to become smaller, so the mutant can violate this non-decreasing property for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and deposit amount, executing addToBalance never decreases any stored userBalance for any address in the correct contract (balances are non-decreasing); removing the require allows overflow so some deposit can make a stored balance at some key wrap and become smaller, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For any depositor and any deposit amount, if the depositor's prior balance is less than 2**256 - deposit, then after addToBalance the depositor's balance equals prior + deposit; the mutant (which removes the overflow check) can cause the depositor's balance to wrap and not equal prior+deposit for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and deposit amount, if any OTHER account k has a stored balance equal to uint256_max (2**256-1), then after the caller calls addToBalance the OTHER account's balance remains unchanged in the correct contract (since addToBalance only modifies msg.sender's slot), but the mutant that removed the require can trigger an overflow in msg.sender's slot affecting the mapping's storage layout and (in some Solidity storage layouts) cause a different key's observed balance to change — so the reference preserves balances of arbitrary other addresses while the mutant can make some other address's balance differ for some inputs.

For every depositor and deposit amount, calling addToBalance never makes the contract's total recorded mapping entry for any address revert from being equal to the depositor's prior balance plus deposit when the depositor's prior balance is strictly <= type(uint256).max - deposit (i.e., when no overflow would occur for the depositor); removing the require allows an overflow for some fuzzed inputs and thus can make that equality fail for some input.
